```{r packages}
library(LDscnR)
library(data.table)
library(SNPRelate)
```

## What problem this solves

A genome scan tests many markers, but nearby markers are often correlated
because they are inherited together. This correlation is **linkage
disequilibrium (LD)**. It describes how alleles co-occur in a sample, and it
is not the same as being physically close on a chromosome or being under
selection. LD can be strong between markers a few hundred base pairs apart,
and around a large inversion or in a region with little recombination it can
extend over many megabases. When several correlated markers all cross a
significance threshold, they are not several independent pieces of evidence.
They are one signal that has been counted several times.

`LDscnR` addresses this in two stages, which this vignette follows in order.

1. **Stage 1** groups markers into **Stage-1 units** from genotype LD alone,
   without the phenotype or any association result. Each unit is then tested
   once, instead of testing every marker.
2. **Stage 2** assembles the significant Stage-1 units into **outlier
   regions**, which are genomic intervals that can be compared with other
   studies.

Two further checks answer questions that the stages cannot answer on their
own. The first asks whether population structure alone could produce about
this many discoveries. This needs a phenotype null that preserves the
structure that matters for the data set at hand, and this vignette builds one
for its own example. The second asks whether the outlier regions overlap
external evidence more often than expected from their size.

The example is `stickleback`, a bundled subset of a three-spined stickleback
panel with 117 fish, about 16,000 markers and three chromosomal regions that
contrast marine and freshwater ecotypes (`?stickleback`). Chromosome 1
carries a well-documented marine-freshwater inversion, which gives the
example a known signal to recover.

```{r cores}
cores <- 2
```

## Stage 1: phenotype-blind Stage-1 units

```{r data}
data("stickleback")
GTs <- stickleback$GTs
map <- copy(stickleback$map)
pheno <- copy(stickleback$pheno)
```

Stage 1 sees only genotypes and marker positions, and never `pheno`. The
units can therefore be built once and reused for any phenotype, and a later
discovery cannot be an artefact of units chosen to fit the answer.

```{r gds}
gds_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".gds")
gds <- create_gds_from_geno(GTs, map, gds_path)
```

```{r ld-decay, results = "hide"}
set.seed(1)
ld_decay <- compute_LD_decay(gds, keep_el = TRUE, slide = 200, n_win_decay = 20, cores = cores)
```

`compute_LD_decay()` fits an LD-decay curve for each chromosome, and
`ld_complexity_reduction()` uses that curve to set each chromosome's LD
cutoff and group markers into Stage-1 units. The mechanics are described in
`vignette("LDscnR_quick_introduction")`. A Stage-1 unit is a set of markers
that are correlated with each other in this data set. It is not a claim that
they form one biological haplotype. Neighbouring units can also still be
somewhat correlated, because the units reduce redundancy but do not make the
tests independent.

```{r stage1, results = "hide"}
stage1 <- ld_complexity_reduction(map = map, LD_decay = ld_decay, r2_rho = 0.5, cores = cores)
```

```{r stage1-show}
stage1
```

## A relationship matrix built the same, phenotype-blind way

Association testing needs a genomic relationship matrix (GRM) to account
for relatedness and population structure. It is built from one
representative marker per Stage-1 unit (`stage1$pruned`) rather than from
every marker, because strongly correlated markers would otherwise carry too
much weight in the relationship estimate.

```{r grm}
K <- snpgdsGRM(gds, snp.id = stage1$pruned, method = "GCTA",
               autosome.only = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, missing.rate = 1)$grm
rownames(K) <- colnames(K) <- rownames(GTs)
```

## One p-value per Stage-1 unit

Each tested unit needs one p-value. This vignette shows the two tests used
in the manuscript.

- **Consensus test.** The genotypes within a unit are averaged into one
  consensus value per individual, which is tested directly. This gives one
  association test per unit. `ld_unit_matrix()` builds these values, and
  `?ld_unit_matrix` lists the other representations it offers.
- **Simes test.** Every marker is tested as usual, and the marker p-values
  within each unit are combined into one size-adjusted p-value.

The consensus test can dilute a signal carried by single markers, whereas
the Simes test is penalised for unit size. Any association method that
returns p-values can be used. Here both tests use `emmax_fast()`, the EMMAX
implementation in LDscnR.

```{r size-floor}
size_floor <- 8L   # illustrative floor for this three-chromosome subset
```

The floor is the minimum number of markers a unit must contain to be
tested. Eight is not a general cutoff. In the manuscript, the floor was set
from marker density, with one required member for every 250 markers per Mb,
rounded and never below two. The full three-spined panel had 2,078 markers
per Mb, which gives a floor of eight. The floor was fixed before any
association or EcoPeak overlap was examined. This subset only demonstrates
the workflow, so it reuses the full-panel floor rather than deriving a new
one.

```{r phenotype}
eco <- as.integer(pheno$ecotype == "Marine")
```

### Consensus testing

```{r consensus-test}
m_cons <- ld_unit_matrix(GTs, stage1, map, size_floor = size_floor, repr = "consensus_dosage")
prep_cons <- emmax_setup(m_cons, K)
p_unit <- emmax_fast(prep_cons, eco)
names(p_unit) <- colnames(m_cons)   # names/order must match attr(m_cons, "units")$unit_id
```

### Simes combination

```{r simes-test}
prep_marker <- emmax_setup(GTs, K)
p_marker <- emmax_fast(prep_marker, eco)
names(p_marker) <- colnames(GTs)   # names/order must match map$marker
```

`p_unit` holds one p-value per tested unit, and `p_marker` holds one
p-value per marker, which `ld_outlier_test()` combines into a Simes p-value
for each unit. Both can be passed to `ld_outlier_test()` unnamed in the
documented order, or named as above. A named vector in the wrong order is
rejected with an error, so a p-value is never matched to the wrong unit or
marker.

## BH correction and Stage-2 assembly

`ld_outlier_test()` applies Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction across
the tested Stage-1 units, so there is one test per unit rather than one per
marker. It then assembles the significant units into outlier regions, which
is Stage 2. Assembly happens after the correction, so it changes how the
significant units are reported but never which units are significant.

```{r outlier-test-consensus}
out_unit <- ld_outlier_test(stage1, map, p_unit, statistic = "unit", size_floor = size_floor,
                            alpha = 0.05, assembly = "physical")
out_unit
```

At the conventional `alpha = 0.05`, no unit is significant after BH
correction. The strongest unit lies on the known chromosome-1 inversion
(21.68 to 21.71 Mb), but its BH-adjusted q-value is about 0.086. This is the
honest result for this small subset, because a known signal can miss a
significance threshold in a modest sample. To show what a positive result
looks like, the rest of this vignette uses `alpha = 0.10`. This is **for
illustration only and not a recommendation**. It recovers exactly one
significant unit, on the inversion.

```{r outlier-test-illustrative}
out_unit <- ld_outlier_test(stage1, map, p_unit, statistic = "unit", size_floor = size_floor,
                            alpha = 0.10, assembly = "stage2_discovered",
                            GTs = GTs, LD_decay = ld_decay)
out_unit
out_unit$regions
```

The Simes test, which starts from marker p-values, agrees that this is the
strongest signal in the data set. Its q-values need not match the consensus
test unit by unit, because it is a different test.

```{r outlier-test-simes}
out_simes <- ld_outlier_test(stage1, map, p_marker, statistic = "simes", size_floor = size_floor,
                             alpha = 0.10, assembly = "stage2_discovered",
                             GTs = GTs, LD_decay = ld_decay)
out_simes$units[significant == TRUE]
```

The default assembly, `assembly = "stage2_discovered"`, clusters only the
significant units with the same LD rule that Stage 1 used, so an outlier
region can only span significant units. `assembly = "physical"` instead
merges significant units that lie close together. It is useful mainly as a
quick check that the two rules broadly agree.

```{r outlier-test-physical}
out_phys <- ld_outlier_test(stage1, map, p_unit, statistic = "unit", size_floor = size_floor,
                            alpha = 0.10, assembly = "physical")
out_phys$regions
```

## Is the observed discovery count unusual?

One significant region does not yet show that population structure alone
could not explain the result. That needs a **null built for the structure of
this data set**. Here the four sampling localities differ in their shares of
marine and freshwater fish, so the null shuffles ecotype **within
locality**. It asks how many discoveries the same workflow would make if
ecotype carried no information beyond locality.

```{r perm-design}
table(pheno$pop_locality, pheno$ecotype)
```

The B permuted phenotypes are drawn once into a fixed matrix rather than
inside each `ld_outlier_perm()` call. This matters because the unit and
region counts are compared below. If each call drew its own permutations,
the comparison would rest on two independent sets of draws rather than on
the same permutations counted in two ways.

```{r perm-run}
B <- 40L
set.seed(1)
p_perm <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  eco_perm <- ave(eco, pheno$pop_locality, FUN = sample)
  emmax_fast(prep_cons, eco_perm)
}, numeric(ncol(m_cons)))

null_units <- ld_outlier_perm(out_unit, stage1, map, p_perm,
                              level = "units", verbose = FALSE)
null_units
```

`null_units$null_obs_ratio` is the **ratio of the mean null count to the
observed count**. It compares how many discoveries the permuted phenotypes
make, on average, with the number this analysis found. It is not a false
discovery rate, and it does not say whether any single region is real. A
small ratio means the observed count is unusual under this null, and a null
built on a different grouping or a continuous structure axis could give a
different answer.

Counts of outlier regions need not agree with counts of significant
units, because assembly can merge several units into one region. Reusing the
same `p_perm` matrix makes this a paired comparison, with both counts taken
from the same permuted phenotypes.

```{r perm-regions}
null_regions <- ld_outlier_perm(out_unit, stage1, map, p_perm, GTs = GTs, LD_decay = ld_decay,
                                level = "regions", verbose = FALSE)
null_regions
identical(null_units$surrogates, null_regions$surrogates)
```

In this run the two counts are identical for every permutation. With a
signal this sparse, no permutation produces more than one significant unit,
so assembly has nothing to merge. This is a property of the small example
and not a general rule. With several significant units, a permutation could
give fewer regions than units, which is why both counts are computed.

## Do the outlier regions overlap external evidence?

The permutation null asks whether the **number of discoveries** is
unusual. A separate question is whether the **outlier regions** overlap
external evidence, such as candidate regions from an independent study or a
gene list, more often than their size alone would predict. The relocation
test in `ld_region_rotation()` answers this question. The two checks do not
replace each other, and a region can pass one and fail the other.

The annotation below is made up for illustration. It has three candidate
intervals, one of which overlaps the inversion region found above, so the
mechanics are visible in a data set this small.

```{r rotation}
chrom_lengths <- map[, .(len = max(Pos)), by = Chr]
annotation <- data.table(
  Chr   = c("Chr1",    "Chr1",    "Chr4"),
  start = c(21690000,  5000000,   8000000),
  end   = c(21700000,  5100000,   8100000)
)
rotation <- ld_region_rotation(out_unit$regions, annotation, chrom_lengths,
                               scheme = "within", n_rotations = 2000, seed = 1)
rotation
```

The test moves each outlier region to a random position on its own
chromosome many times, keeping its span unchanged. It then asks how often
the relocated regions overlap the annotation at least as much as the
observed regions do. Each region is placed independently, and the resulting
fold enrichment measures something different from the permutation null
above.

## Summary

- Stage 1 (`ld_complexity_reduction()`) groups markers into phenotype-blind
  Stage-1 units.
- `ld_unit_matrix()` turns each unit into one consensus variable for the
  consensus test, while the Simes test combines marker p-values. In both
  cases `ld_outlier_test()` applies BH correction once across the tested
  units.
- Stage 2 assembles the significant units into outlier regions after the
  correction.
- `ld_outlier_perm()` asks whether the number of discoveries is unusual under
  a null that preserves the structure of the data set. It reports a ratio of
  null to observed counts and a count-based p-value, not a per-region
  statement or a false discovery rate.
- `ld_region_rotation()` runs the relocation test, which asks whether the
  outlier regions overlap external evidence more than their size alone would
  predict.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
SNPRelate::snpgdsClose(gds)
unlink(gds_path)
```
